# Discussion

We asked whether the structural connectome, through any of its candidate communication
routes, explains cortical atrophy in AD and FTD beyond spatial proximity, and whether the
answer differs between these two spatially distinct diseases. Three findings stand out.

**First, proximity along the cortex explains most of the atrophy topography in both
diseases.** A single-parameter spatial kernel predicted each region's atrophy from other
regions better than any structural communication model, and geodesic distance did better
than Euclidean distance. This argues against the concern that a Euclidean baseline is
inflated by bridging sulci and fissures: the smoothness of atrophy follows the cortical sheet.
This is compatible with several mechanisms that our data cannot separate, including
spread between neighbouring cortical columns, shared vulnerability of neighbouring regions
with similar cytoarchitecture and gene expression, and the spatial smoothing inherent in
DBM and group statistics.

**Second, the structural connectome adds little beyond its own geometry.** Direct
connections, shortest paths, communicability, search information, navigation and network
diffusion all correlated with atrophy, but none survived a null that preserves the map's
spatial autocorrelation (variogram-matched surrogates) or one that preserves the
connectome's wiring geometry (with a bin-width-dependent exception for path-based models in
bvFTD), and none outperformed the distance kernel, including when
given the same freedom to fit. Seeded network diffusion on the SC, evaluated in its
generative form as recommended, was never better than isotropic spread from the same seed.
Adding the hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus and striatum did not change this in AD, although
every AD model chose the bilateral amygdala as the seed. The only structural signal beyond
geometry was in bvFTD: path-based models survived geometry-preserving rewiring with coarse
bins, and search information retained a small long-range contribution beyond distance. These results do
not show that pathology does not travel along axons. They show that, at the resolution of
group-level atrophy maps and a young-adult tractography connectome, the information in the
structural connectome that is relevant to atrophy is largely the information in its spatial
layout, which neighbouring cortex already carries.

**Third, FTD follows the long-range functional architecture more strongly than AD.** When
nearby regions were excluded, thresholded FC predicted bvFTD and pooled FTD atrophy far
better than distance, under every spatial null and at every resolution; svPPA and nfvPPA
showed weaker versions of the same effect. In AD the unique long-range functional
contribution was about half as large, and in MCI it was small. This dissociation fits the view of bvFTD as a
disorder of a distributed salience/limbic network [1, 2, 5] whose nodes are far apart but
functionally coupled, whereas the AD map at this group level is captured by bilateral,
medial temporal-centred spread along the cortex. The FC effect was carried by the strongest
functional connections: proportional thresholding raised it substantially, as expected if
weak, globally shared correlations add noise rather than signal.

**Methodological implications.** The conclusion about the structural connectome depends
almost entirely on the null model. Degree-preserving rewiring roughly doubles the mean
connection length and makes any spatially smooth map look network-constrained. Parcel-level
spins make surrogates rougher at short range than real maps and are liberal for statistics
based on neighbours, as anticipated by Markello and Mišić [19]. We recommend that studies of
network-constrained atrophy (i) report a fitted spatial baseline, preferably geodesic;
(ii) use at least one null that preserves short-range autocorrelation (variogram or Moran)
and one that preserves wiring geometry, while noting that geometry-preserving rewiring is
conservative because it cannot move about half of the edges; (iii) refit every free
parameter inside each null; (iv) count only positive fits as support; and (v) check
hemispheric effects with homotopic comparisons, because standard parcellations are not
left–right symmetric. The negative association between FC strength and atrophy in FTD was
not explained by a template-based dropout proxy, but HCP-specific susceptibility loss in
orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex [35] can only be excluded with the HCP's own
signal maps, so we do not interpret it as hub sparing.

**Limitations.** The maps are group averages from different cohorts and pipelines (ADNI and
NIFD), so between-disease differences mix disease with cohort effects; the three FTD-variant
maps probably share controls and are on an unconfirmed scale (we have asked the authors).
The connectomes come from young healthy adults, tractography under-samples some
temporo-limbic and commissural tracts, and FC is affected by signal dropout. DBM measures
volume change of the deformation, which includes ventricular expansion; we mitigated this for
subcortical structures by sampling their core, but the caudate remains unreliable. Only the
cortex has geodesic distances; the subcortical analyses use Euclidean distances and spins
cannot be applied to the subcortex, so we relied on variogram and Moran nulls there. No
cortical-thickness maps for these diseases were available to test whether the results depend
on DBM; individual-level and longitudinal data are needed to move from group topography to
spreading dynamics.

**Conclusion.** Across AD and FTD, cortical atrophy is organised mainly by proximity along
the cortical sheet, and structural communication models do not explain it beyond that
geometry. A long-range functional-network component is clearly present in bvFTD and FTD and
weak in AD. Claims of connectome-constrained atrophy should be tested against fitted spatial
baselines and geometry-aware nulls.
